steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Six real games in our archive start the same way. What did the knight sacrifice buy, where did each game turn, and when is a weapon like this worth playing? Afterwards you can explain it to a friend and meet it from the Black side. steps.text: **What White hopes for.** [I] The knight on e5 pressures g6 and f7. Black's e-pawns are doubled, so e6 is a target. Black's kingside is clumsy: the bishop needs a square, and the knight on g8 and rook on h8 are shut in. The sacrifice is a bet that this clumsiness will cost Black more than the knight cost White. Test the first claim: which squares does the knight attack?

steps.text: **The practical secret.** [V] All six Black players retreated the bishop to f7, a move the engine rates lower than the retreat to f5 by roughly six tenths of a pawn. [I] A surprise weapon pays when the natural reply is the inaccurate one. The sacrifice costs White about 1.6 pawns against the quiet alternative; the weapon works because the first error often belongs to the other side. Keep that in mind in the three model games.

steps.text: **Where game 2 turned.** [I] The rook sent to h7 by the knight spent several moves there, the bishop retreat on move 10 put the bishop on a passive corner square, and Black castled only on move 19. The finish was a mate on the back rank, which only existed because the king was boxed in by its own pawns.

steps.text: **What game 3 teaches.** [V] White's advantage went from more than four pawns at move 20 to roughly nothing by move 30. [I] When the attack stops, the evaluation goes with it: the score was never extra material. A surprise weapon builds its advantage early; to keep it the player must know the positions it leads to, including endgames. Two of the six games in our file were lost by White, and this loss came from a winning position.

steps.text: **Why a surprise weapon scores.** [I] Three reasons. First, the natural reply may be the inaccurate one (six out of six here). Second, the defender has no prepared answer and must calculate on their own clock. Third, the attacker knows the structure well. [H] The shorter the time limit, the larger the first two effects. Our six games are too few to test it.
steps.chapter: When to use it, and the Black defence

steps.text: **Why learn the defence too.** [I] Meeting the line is easier than playing it if you know three rules. Take the knight. Retreat the bishop to f5 and not f7. Count attackers and defenders on f7 and e6 before every move. We check each rule with the engine on the next boards.

steps.prompt: Predict for each position, then check. One difference matters; one does not.

steps.text: **A typical mistake, and why it fails.** [I] Black develops the queen's knight to d7 to challenge the knight on e5. It fails when White's queen can join the attack on e6 in one move after Nxf7 Kxf7: then e6 has one defender against two attackers. The same move is fine when the queen needs two moves (model game 2). Test it on a board, then find the better move yourself.

steps.text: **Recap: what to remember.** The line is a bet: the engine prefers a quiet knight move and scores the sacrifice lower. It pays when the natural bishop retreat is the inaccurate one; the retreat to f5 is rated about six tenths of a pawn better. In the model games, count attackers and defenders on e6, and watch the back rank and the b5-e8 diagonal. A won position still has to be converted. Six games are too few to judge the line.

Self-check afterwards: did you say how many games, that the higher-rated player won five of the six, did you give an example, did you name a mistake? The app grades nothing; compare with the recap.
